findings.title: --set-default switches off the default-entry restore on the FAILURE path too: a `make install` that dies or is interrupted after 20-grub.install leaves the machine defaulting to a kernel with no initramfs
findings.location: install_kernel, lines 2807-2821 (condition at 2815-2816)
findings.scenario: The build running right now uses profile xeon-haswell-all-gpu-server-latency.ini, which has install = yes AND set_default = yes, so it reaches this code with set_default=True. (1) `sudo make ... install` -> /sbin/installkernel is kernel-install here -> 20-grub.install copies vmlinuz, writes the BLS entry and immediately runs `grub2-editenv - set saved_entry=<new>` (grub2-get-kernel-settings prints GRUB_UPDATE_DEFAULT_KERNEL=true on this machine; the release contains none of 64k|auto|rt|uki). (2) 50-dracut.install then fails (`exit $ret`, non-zero -> kernel-install fails -> make fails -> ToolError), or the user presses ^C / the ssh session drops during the ~1 minute dracut runs. (3) The finally block is guarded by `not opts["set_default"]`, so nothing is restored; the later set_default() call is never reached, but the hook already moved the default. Result: saved_entry points at an entry whose initramfs does not exist; root here is xfs on LVM, so the next (default) boot panics and needs someone at the console to pick another entry. The code comment calls this 'the one failure that must not also skip the restore', and the unit test covers it only for set_default=False.

  set_default=True : install failed ... default boot entry afterwards: vmlinuz-new [LEFT ON THE NEW KERNEL THAT HAS NO INITRAMFS]
/usr/lib/kernel/install.d/20-grub.install: `if [ -n "$NEWDEFAULT" ]; then grub2-editenv - set "saved_entry=${NEWDEFAULT}"; fi` runs before 40-dkms/50-dracut; 50-dracut.install ends with `exit $ret`.
Live profile: `install = yes`, `set_default = yes`.
findings.suggested_fix:
Track completion and restore whenever the install did not complete:

  try: sudo(modules_install); sudo(install); done = True
  finally:
      if old_default and not dry and (not opts["set_default"] or not done) and grubby_default() != old_default: set_default(old_default) ...
Add the set_default=True variant of test_default_entry_is_put_back_even_when_make_install_fails.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute it. The guard in install_kernel's finally block (lines 2815-2816) is `if old_default and not opts["set_default"] and not dry and grubby_default() != old_default:`. With set_default=True that condition is false on every path, including the failure path. The later `set_default("/boot/vmlinuz-" + release)` at 2833 is never reached when `sudo(... install)` raises. So the default stays wherever installkernel's hook left it.

The hook does what the finder says on this machine:
- /sbin/installkernel is a symlink to kernel-install (systemd 257).
- /usr/lib/kernel/install.d/20-grub.install runs `grub2-editenv - set "saved_entry=${NEWDEFAULT}"`. It runs before 40-dkms and 50-dracut, and 50-dracut ends with `exit $ret`.
- /etc/sysconfig/kernel has UPDATEDEFAULT=yes, and grub2-get-kernel-settings prints GRUB_UPDATE_DEFAULT_KERNEL=true.
- The live release 7.2.6-xeon-haswell-all-gpu-server-latency does not match `64k|auto|rt|uki` (checked with the same grep), so the hook moves the default.
- The live profile has `install = yes` and `set_default = yes`.

The user's build finished and installed while I was reviewing. The second-session log test-runs/first-real-install-2026-09-20.txt shows the window: at 08:07:45 vmlinuz was in /boot and the initramfs was not; the initramfs appeared at 08:08:52. A dracut failure, ^C or SIGHUP in that minute would have left saved_entry on a kernel with no initramfs, on an xfs-on-LVM root, and nothing would have put it back.

One detail the finder did not need: 40-dkms.install always exits 0, so a DKMS failure is not a trigger. Only a dracut failure, another hook failing, or an interrupt is.

Severity stays critical. The outcome is a default boot entry that panics, on the path the user's own profile takes. It is mitigated because it needs a second failure and the old kernel can still be picked at the console. The unit test covers the failure path only for set_default=False.

findings.title: `install --source TREE` never looks at the recorded state: it installs from a tree that is mid-build, failed at the build stage, or reconfigured after its last build
findings.location: built_tree lines 3821-3823; cmd_install lines 3838-3841
findings.scenario: built_tree() returns opts["source"] before any status filter, and cmd_install only requires that vmlinux and include/config/kernel.release exist. The live tree is exactly such a case now: state.ini says `status = building`, .config was rewritten 07:34 (modules=full, debug_info=btf), kernel.release 07:35, while vmlinux/bzImage are from the PREVIOUS build (06:16/06:17). `install --source ~/src/linux-7.2.6` at this moment (or after that build fails half way) passes every check: post_build_checks reads the old modules.order, then `sudo make modules_install` does `rm -fr /lib/modules/<rel>/kernel` and copies whatever mix of old and freshly rebuilt .ko exists (CONFIG_MODVERSIONS=y: CRCs of new modules need not match the old image), `make install` installs the stale bzImage, and the NEW .config is copied to /boot/config-<rel> although it does not describe that image. If LOCALVERSION changed, kernel.release already holds the new string while the image still reports the old one, so the initramfs is built for a release the image will never look for. With --set-default that entry becomes the default. Same for a tree left at status=configured by --configure-only.
findings.evidence:
Experiment (scratch/exp2.py: fake tree, temp --state-dir, --dry-run, state set to building / failed@build / configured, state release=7.2.6-new, kernel.release on disk=7.2.6-old): all three runs print `release : 7.2.6-old`, `would run: sudo make -j24 -C .../linux-fake modules_install`, `would run: sudo make -C .../linux-fake install`, `would run: sudo install -m 0644 .../.config /boot/config-7.2.6-old`, exit code 0. No mention of the recorded status.
Live state.ini: `[/home/madness/src/linux-7.2.6] status = building, stage = build`; `ls -l`: vmlinux Sep 20 06:16, bzImage 06:17, .config 07:34.
findings.suggested_fix: In cmd_install, after resolving the tree: s = state.get(tree); refuse (with a message naming the status) when s.get("status") in ("configuring", "building", "configured") or (s.get("status") == "failed" and s.get("stage") in ("configure", "build")), and when s.get("release") differs from kernel.release on disk. Trees with no section (built by hand / legacy script) stay allowed. Better still, one flock per tree held by build, package and install (package --source on a tree being built would start a second make in it).

verdict.reasoning:
There is no guard. built_tree() starts with `if opts["source"]: return opts["source"]` (3822-3823), before the status filter. cmd_install's only tree test is `if not release or not os.path.isfile(os.path.join(tree, "vmlinux")): raise` (3839-3841). Nothing in cmd_install, post_build_checks, install_preflight or install_kernel reads state status or stage; install_kernel reads only `state.get(tree).get("debug_info")`.

kbuild does not protect root either. In the 7.2.6 tree:
- `no-sync-config-targets := ... %install ...` (Makefile:302), so install targets do not sync the config.
- arch/x86/Makefile:311-313: `install:` has no prerequisite, so whatever bzImage is there gets installed.
- scripts/Makefile.modinst:17 runs `$(shell rm -fr $(MODLIB)/kernel $(MODLIB)/build)` before copying.
So a stale image, a mixed module set and the new .config are installed exactly as the finder describes.

The finder's live snapshot (status=building, vmlinux older than .config) was accurate when taken. It is now history: the build finished at 08:08:54.

Severity stays medium. It needs the user to point --source at a tree whose last recorded run did not finish building, which is unlikely. The result is a kernel entry whose modules and config do not match its image, and it becomes the default with --set-default.
verdict.experiment:
ins2.py uses a fake tree in scratch, a temp --state-dir and --dry-run. post_build_checks is stubbed so no probe make runs, and a guard asserts no real sudo. State is set to building, failed/build, configured and configuring in turn, with state release=7.2.6-new and kernel.release on disk=7.2.6-old. Read-only in the real tree: the Makefile and modinst lines quoted in the reasoning.
verdict.minimal_fix:
In cmd_install, right after `tree = built_tree(opts, state)`:

    s = state.get(tree)
    unfinished = s.get("status") in ("configuring", "building", "configured") or \
        (s.get("status") == "failed" and s.get("stage") in ("configure", "build"))
    if unfinished:
        raise ToolError("%s is recorded as '%s%s': what is in it was not produced by a finished build.\n"
                        "  Run `build --source %s` first (incremental), then install."
                        % (tree, s.get("status"), " at " + s["stage"] if s.get("stage") else "", tree))

Trees with no section (built by hand or by the legacy script) stay allowed.

1. Make the release comparison (state `release` vs kernel.release) a warn(), not a refusal. cmd_build writes the predicted release before the build, so a legitimately hand-rebuilt tree would otherwise be locked out.
2. Do not add --yes as the override; see INS-3. The message should name `build --source` as the way forward.

findings.title: --yes silently disables four unrelated guards, and every refusal message recommends it
findings.location: install_preflight lines 2735, 2747, 2753; cmd_build line 3798; cmd_install line 3851
findings.scenario: --yes overrides (a) failed post-build checks, (b) 'the release being installed is the kernel running now', (c) 'Secure Boot is ON and your certificate is not enrolled', (d) no initramfs generator. Only (d) says so when bypassed. Concrete: the user boots the kernel this profile installs (fixed localversion), rebuilds it, a DKMS probe fails, the message says '`install --yes` overrides'. They run `install --yes` for THAT reason; line 2735 is then skipped without a word and `make modules_install` does `rm -fr /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/kernel` under the live kernel. On a Secure-Boot-on machine the same --yes skips the MOK check and the tool still prints `ok Secure Boot here: on`; with --set-default the default entry is then one shim will refuse.
findings.evidence: Line 2735: `if release and release == machine["running"] and not opts["yes"]: raise` (nothing printed when yes). Line 2747: `if k and mok_enrolled(k) is False and not opts["yes"]: raise`, followed unconditionally by `ok("Secure Boot here: %s")`. Messages: '--yes overrides', 'pass --yes to do it anyway', '--yes installs anyway', 'or --yes to go ahead'.
findings.suggested_fix: Smallest: when a guard is bypassed by --yes, warn() exactly what was bypassed (running-kernel overwrite, certificate not enrolled, N failed checks) before sudo is touched. Cleaner: keep --yes for failed post-build checks only and add --replace-running / --not-enrolled style flags named in the respective messages.

verdict.reasoning:
Confirmed as a design flaw with a misleading message. The lines are as quoted by the finder:
- 2735: `if release and release == machine["running"] and not opts["yes"]: raise ...`. Nothing is printed when --yes skips it.
- 2747: `if k and mok_enrolled(k) is False and not opts["yes"]: raise ...`, followed unconditionally by `ok("Secure Boot here: %s" ...)`.
- 2753: the no-initramfs guard. It is the only one that says so when bypassed: `none (--yes given)`.
- 3798 and 3851: `if problems and not opts["yes"]`.

Every refusal message recommends --yes: `install --yes overrides`, `pass --yes to do it anyway`, `--yes installs anyway`, `or --yes to go ahead`. The flag's help text is `do not stop for confirmations`.

The cross-over scenario is real. In cmd_build the post-build-problems refusal (3798) is raised before install_kernel and therefore before install_preflight(release). A user whose fixed-localversion kernel is the running one sees only `install --yes overrides`. Running `install --yes` then skips line 2735 without a word. That describes this user after one reboot: the profile has a fixed localversion and that release was installed today.

It is not worse than medium. Each guard's own message offers --yes as its override, nothing is destroyed beyond what that guard already warns about, and the default entry is not touched without --set-default.
verdict.experiment:
ins3.py calls the real install_preflight with a key in a temp XDG_CONFIG_HOME, mok_enrolled stubbed to False, machine secure_boot=on, running equal to the release, and no initramfs tool.
  --yes=False -> refused: the release being installed (7.2.6-same) is the kernel running now.
  --yes=True -> PASSED
The complete output with --yes was three lines: `ok Secure Boot here: on`, `ok initramfs generator: none (--yes given)`, `ok /boot has 10.0 GB free`. There was no mention of the running-kernel overwrite or of the certificate not being enrolled.

findings.title: Secure Boot gate identifies 'my key' by a substring match on the certificate CN: an empty CN passes any image, and a regenerated key (same CN) makes an image signed by the OLD key pass a MOK check done on the NEW certificate
findings.location: install_preflight line 2742 (compare sign_image line 2644, signing_key lines 2579-2601)
findings.scenario: A) sign_image guards with `if cn and cn in ...`; install_preflight does not. If key_cn() returns '' (secureboot.crt unreadable/corrupt), `'' in image_signers(img)` is True for every image, including an unsigned one, so `signed` is True and the refusal is skipped. B) CN is always '<user>@<host> kernel signing key'. signing_key() regenerates ALL THREE files (overwriting the private key) when any one is missing - e.g. after the user MOVES secureboot.der next to a package, as README/PLAN tell them to hand it out. The next sign/build/package makes key B with the same CN; sign_image answers 'already' for the image that carries A's signature; the user enrols B as instructed; the gate then sees CN match + mok_enrolled(B) True and installs a kernel whose only signature (A) is not in MOK. With Secure Boot on, shim refuses it; with --set-default that is the default entry.
findings.evidence:
Experiment (scratch/exp4.py, keys in a temp XDG_CONFIG_HOME, a copy of /boot/vmlinuz-7.2.4-gpu as the image):
  key A: madness@siege3 kernel signing key 82:14:50:...
  sign with A -> signed
  signing_key(create=False) with the .der gone -> None
  key B: madness@siege3 kernel signing key 3E:C7:C3:...  (new private key, A overwritten)
  sign with B -> already
  GATE PASSED: image signed by A only, MOK holds B only
  key_cn with an unreadable .crt -> ''
  GATE PASSED with an image that is NOT signed by this key (signers of that image: [])
findings.suggested_fix: Line 2742: `cn = key_cn(k) if k else ""; signed = bool(cn and img and os.path.isfile(img) and cn in image_signers(img))`. Make the CN unique per key (append e.g. 8 hex digits of a random serial at creation) so 'already' and the gate cannot match another key. In signing_key(): if secureboot.key exists never regenerate - rebuild only the .der from the .crt, and raise if .key or .crt is missing while the other exists.

verdict.reasoning:
Both halves reproduced.

A) Line 2742 is `signed = bool(k and img and os.path.isfile(img) and key_cn(k) in image_signers(img))`. There is no `cn and` guard, unlike sign_image at 2644 (`if cn and cn in ...`) and 2666. key_cn() returns '' when openssl cannot parse the .crt, and `'' in <any str>` is True. An image pesign reports as `No signatures found.` therefore passes as signed.

B) signing_key() lines 2579-2593: `if all(os.path.isfile(v) for v in k.values()): return k`. Otherwise it runs `openssl req ... -keyout k["key"] -out k["crt"]`. If any one of the three files is missing, the private key is overwritten. That includes the .der, which is derived, and which README and PLAN tell the user to hand out. The CN is always `<user>@<host> kernel signing key`, so the new key cannot be told apart from the old one by CN. sign_image answers `already`, and the gate passes an image that carries only the old key's signature.

The key overwrite is the more serious part. It silently destroys a private key that other machines may have enrolled; the only output is `made a Secure Boot signing key`.

Severity stays medium. Both halves need an unlikely precondition: a file removed from or corrupted in the keys directory. The gate only matters where Secure Boot is on. cmd_package's packaged_image_signed() has the same `cn in ...` pattern, but it is not reachable with an empty CN, because signing fails first on a corrupt .crt.

    signed = bool(cn and img and os.path.isfile(img) and cn in image_signers(img))

findings.title: ^C / SIGHUP / SIGTERM after the build has finished records the tree as 'failed', so `install`, `package`, `sign`, `pin` without --source silently pick an OLDER tree (or none)
findings.location: cmd_build lines 3804-3806; built_tree lines 3824-3829
findings.scenario: The `except Exception` branch keeps status='built' for stages after the build ('built must survive a failure that came after it'), but `except KeyboardInterrupt` writes status='failed' for ANY stage. main() maps SIGTERM and SIGHUP to KeyboardInterrupt. So: build finishes (status=built), the user presses ^C during the slow DKMS probes or at the second sudo prompt, or the ssh session drops during `sudo make install` -> status=failed, stage=checks|install. built_tree() only accepts built/installing/installed, so the next `install` (no --source) takes the most recently finished OTHER tree - e.g. the old 7.2.4 tree - prints its name and goes straight on to sudo; with no other tree it says 'no built tree on record'.
findings.evidence:
Code: `except KeyboardInterrupt: state.update(tree, status="failed", stage=stage, exit_code=130, finished=now())` (no stage test, unlike lines 3810-3814).
Experiment (scratch/exp6.py part B): before the interrupt built_tree -> .../linux-7.2.6; after the same state.update cmd_build performs -> .../linux-7.2.4 '<- the OLDER tree'.
findings.suggested_fix: Mirror the Exception branch: `if stage in ("configure", "build"): state.update(... status="failed" ...) else: state.update(tree, last_error="%s: interrupted" % stage)`. In cmd_install, when the tree was chosen by built_tree() rather than --source and is not the newest section in the state file, ask/confirm or refuse.

verdict.reasoning:
Lines 3804-3806 are `except KeyboardInterrupt: state.update(tree, status="failed", stage=stage, exit_code=130, finished=now()); raise`. There is no stage test. The `except Exception` branch just below (3810-3814) keeps `built` for stages after the build, with the comment "'built' must survive a failure that came after it". main() maps SIGTERM and SIGHUP to KeyboardInterrupt (4194-4195).

built_tree() accepts only `("built", "installing", "installed")` (3825). After an interrupt during the DKMS probes or during install, the freshly built tree is invisible to install, package, sign, pin and dkms-check when they are run without --source.

The damage is limited:
- decide_clean treats `failed` as incremental, so nothing is cleaned.
- With a single tree on record the user gets `no built tree on record -- pass --source`, which is recoverable.
- With an older built tree on record, `install` picks it, prints `tree`/`release`, and continues to sudo without asking. If that older release is the running kernel, the line-2735 guard stops it; otherwise an older kernel is reinstalled.

One interaction with INS-8: when the interrupt arrives while a sudo child is alive, it surfaces as PermissionError. That goes to the Exception branch and keeps the status, so the wrong `failed` is recorded mainly for interrupts during the checks stage or at a prompt.
verdict.experiment:
ins5.py drives the real cmd_build through main() with the slow steps stubbed (detect, toolchain, configure, run_build) and a temp --state-dir. An older tree linux-7.2.4 is recorded as installed. post_build_checks raises KeyboardInterrupt, as ^C during the probes would.
  main() returned 130; recorded: status=failed stage=checks exit_code=130
  built_tree() -> .../ins5/linux-7.2.4 (the older tree)

findings.title: When grubby exists but cannot name the current default, the install goes ahead, nothing is restored, and the closing hint implies the default was left alone
findings.location: install_kernel lines 2795-2797 and 2837-2839; grubby_default lines 2768-2777
findings.scenario: grubby_default() returns '' whenever no output line is an existing file as seen by the unprivileged user: saved_entry names a removed entry (this grubby then prints a bash 'bad array subscript' error), the default is a UKI/type-2 entry, /boot is mode 0700, or sudo could not run grubby. install_kernel treats '' as 'nothing to restore' and carries on. 20-grub.install (UPDATEDEFAULT=yes) makes the new kernel the default; the finally block is skipped because old_default is ''; the tool then prints 'pick <rel> from the boot menu; once it has proved itself: sudo grubby --set-default=...'. README: 'It will refuse to ... change your default boot entry without --set-default'. The user reboots expecting the old kernel and gets the unproven one.
findings.evidence: Experiment (scratch/exp6.py part A: fake sudo, grubby --default-kernel returns an error line, make install moves saved_entry): output is only 'pick 7.2.6-elkt from the boot menu; once it has proved itself: ...' and 'saved_entry afterwards: NEW-ID (no --set-default was given; no warning was printed)'.
findings.suggested_fix: If grubby is present and old_default == '' (and not dry, not --set-default): stop before `make install` with 'cannot determine the current default boot entry' (or at least warn). After the install, in the non-set-default branch, call grubby_default() once more and warn loudly if it now equals /boot/vmlinuz-<release>.

verdict.reasoning:
grubby_default() (2772-2777) accepts only a line for which `line.startswith("/") and os.path.isfile(line)` holds, as seen by the unprivileged user; otherwise it returns ''. install_kernel then does `old_default = grubby_default(dry) if grubby else ""` and `if old_default: info(...)`. An empty result is treated as nothing to restore. The finally guard starts with `if old_default and`. The closing branch `elif grubby:` prints `pick %s from the boot menu; once it has proved itself: sudo grubby --set-default=...`, which tells the user the default was left alone.

The precondition is natural on EL. /usr/sbin/grubby's get_default_index() echoes nothing when saved_entry matches no BLS entry. display_default_value then evaluates `${bls_linux[$default_index]}` with an empty index, giving bash `bad array subscript`, prints the prefix `/boot`, and exits 0. Neither output line is an existing file. 20-grub.install's `remove)` branch deletes the BLS entry and vmlinuz but never touches saved_entry. So `kernel-install remove <old custom kernel that was the default>`, which is the normal way to remove a kernel that is not RPM-managed, leaves exactly this state.

Mitigation for that particular case: grub already falls back to entry 0, usually the newest kernel, so the real change is small and the main fault is the misleading message. In the other cases the finder lists, a valid old default really is replaced silently, contrary to README line 185 (`change your default boot entry without --set-default`):
- /boot mode 0700, so isfile() is False for the unprivileged user;
- a UKI default outside the user's view.
verdict.experiment:
ins6.py runs the real install_kernel against a fake sudo with set_default=False; the fake `make install` moves saved_entry.
  (a) grubby output `/usr/sbin/grubby: line 123: ... bad array subscript` -> grubby_default() returns ''; saved_entry afterwards: NEW-ID; restore attempts: 0; warnings printed: 0. The only related output is `pick 7.2.6-elkt from the boot menu; once it has proved itself: sudo grubby --set-default=/boot/vmlinuz-7.2.6-elkt`.
  (b) grubby names a path the user cannot stat -> identical result.

Read-only: /usr/sbin/grubby lines 111-157 and 20-grub.install's remove branch, which contains no saved_entry handling.
verdict.minimal_fix:
Warn rather than refuse. Refusing would block every install for a user whose saved_entry dangles, and there is nothing valid to restore to in that case. In install_kernel after line 2795:

    unknown_default = bool(grubby and not old_default and not dry and not opts["set_default"])
    if unknown_default:
        warn("cannot tell which boot entry is the default now (grubby named no kernel): it CANNOT be put back if installkernel moves it")

Replace the closing hint: `elif grubby and unknown_default: warn("the default boot entry may now be %s -- check `sudo grubby --default-kernel` before you reboot" % release)`; keep the existing `elif grubby:` text otherwise.

The `not dry` matters: in a dry run grubby_default always returns ''. The unit tests are unaffected because their fake grubby names an existing file.

Optional hardening for /boot mode 0700: in grubby_default also accept a line matching r"^/\S*/vmlinuz-\S+$" when os.path.isfile cannot see it.

verdict.experiment:
ins7.py calls the real install_preflight with a temp XDG_CONFIG_HOME, mok_enrolled stubbed to False, and secure_boot=on.
  early call as cmd_build makes it (no release, no key yet): PASSED
  after the build, SB on, key now exists, not enrolled: REFUSED: Secure Boot is ON here and your signing certificate is not enrolled

verdict.minimal_fix:
(a) After line 3750 (`info("release : %s" % predicted)`), repeat only the one check. This avoids printing the three `ok` lines a second time:

    if opts["install"] and predicted == machine["running"] and not opts["yes"]:
        raise ToolError(<the same message as line 2736>)

The except branch records status=failed, stage=configure for a tree that may have been `installed`, and that hides it from built_tree(). To avoid it, write the refusal as state last_error and return 1 instead of raising, or move `stage = "build"` below the check and special-case it. The .config has already been committed by then, so recording `failed at configure` is defensible.

(b) In the early call, make the key before checking: in install_preflight use `k = signing_key(create=(opts.get("secure_boot", "on") == "on" and not tree))` when machine["secure_boot"] == "on", so mok_enrolled() has a real certificate to test. findings.title: ^C or SIGTERM while a sudo child is running turns into an uncaught PermissionError traceback (subprocess.run tries to SIGKILL root-owned sudo)
findings.location: run lines 137-142; sudo line 2729; main lines 4209-4214
findings.scenario: sudo makes itself fully root so the invoking user cannot signal it. On KeyboardInterrupt, subprocess.run waits 0.25 s, then calls process.kill(); os.kill on sudo raises PermissionError(EPERM), which replaces the KeyboardInterrupt. At a terminal this happens whenever the child does not die within 0.25 s (dracut cleaning its temp dir); with SIGTERM/SIGHUP sent to the tool alone it happens always, after the tool has blocked until `sudo make install` finished. run() catches only FileNotFoundError and TimeoutExpired, main() only ToolError and KeyboardInterrupt, so the user gets a Python traceback and exit 1 instead of 'interrupted' / 130. The restore in install_kernel's finally still runs.
findings.evidence: Experiment (scratch/exp5.py: os.kill patched to raise EPERM for other pids as the kernel does for sudo, SIGTERM via the tool's own _as_interrupt handler while elkt.run(['sleep','4'], interactive=True) runs): 'PermissionError after 4.0s: [Errno 1] Operation not permitted -> NOT caught by main()'.
findings.suggested_fix: In run(): `except PermissionError as e: if e.errno == errno.EPERM and cmd and cmd[0] == "sudo": raise KeyboardInterrupt(); raise`. Or start sudo children with Popen and, on KeyboardInterrupt, wait() for them instead of kill().

verdict.reasoning:
run() (137-142) catches only FileNotFoundError and subprocess.TimeoutExpired. main() (4209-4214) catches only ToolError and KeyboardInterrupt.

The platform Python is 3.12.14, and I quoted its source. subprocess.run has `except: # Including KeyboardInterrupt, communicate handled that. process.kill(); raise`. Popen.send_signal suppresses only ProcessLookupError around `os.kill(self.pid, sig)`. sudo makes itself fully root before running the command (sudo.c: `Become full root (not just setuid) so user cannot kill us`), so os.kill on it from the invoking user gives EPERM. The PermissionError replaces the KeyboardInterrupt. Popen.__exit__ then sees a non-KeyboardInterrupt exception and does a blocking wait(), so the tool hangs until `sudo make install` finishes. After that a traceback reaches the user, with exit 1 instead of the `interrupted` message and 130. Python 3.6's subprocess.run takes the same path.

At a terminal this happens only when the sudo child survives the 0.25 s grace period (_sigint_wait_secs), which is plausible while dracut cleans up. With SIGTERM or SIGHUP delivered to the tool alone it always happens.

The finder is right that install_kernel's finally still runs. Secondary effect: in cmd_build the PermissionError lands in `except Exception`, so state gets a last_error rather than the interrupt record.

Severity is low: the restore still runs, and the defect is the traceback and the wrong exit code. I did not run a real sudo (hard rule). The EPERM is simulated; that is the only assumption, and it is sudo's documented behaviour.
verdict.experiment:
ins8.py puts a fake `sudo` first on PATH (a scratch script: exec "$@"). os.kill is patched to raise PermissionError(EPERM) for any pid but our own, as the kernel does for a root-owned sudo. elkt.main() is driven with a command that calls the real elkt.sudo(["sleep","3"]), and SIGTERM is sent to the tool after 0.5 s through the tool's own _as_interrupt handler.
  Original: `main() let PermissionError escape after 3.0s: [Errno 1] Operation not permitted (context: KeyboardInterrupt)`. It blocked until the child ended and the exception was not caught.
  Patched copy: `main() returned 130 after 3.0s: ['interrupted -- ...']`. 111 tests pass.
verdict.minimal_fix:
The finder's snippet would raise NameError, because the tool does not import `errno`. PermissionError alone is enough. In run(), after the TimeoutExpired clause:

    except PermissionError:
        # ^C/SIGTERM while sudo runs: subprocess.run() tries to SIGKILL a child that made itself root
        if cmd and cmd[0] == "sudo":
            raise KeyboardInterrupt()
        raise

The `cmd[0] == "sudo"` test keeps a genuine EACCES from an unexecutable compiler path a real error. Popen.__exit__ has already waited for the sudo child by then. That is the desirable behaviour for `make install`, since root's make is not abandoned half way.

Tested on the scratch copy. It is Python 3.6 safe: PermissionError exists since 3.3 and the 3.6 run() takes the same path.

lenses.dropped_note:
Seven smaller issues dropped (all low severity):

1. **O= build.** A goal-less `make O=dir` from the tree still triggers the hook. It runs `sign --source $(CURDIR)`, which is the source tree, not the output directory. The build therefore ends with "bzImage does not exist" and Error 1, or a stale in-tree image gets signed. The hook condition lacks `$(O)$(KBUILD_OUTPUT)`.

2. **Special characters in paths.**
   - The tool's own path with a space: `$(wildcard ...)` sees two words, so the hook is silently off. `package` then fails late with the misleading "was it removed?" message. Verified.
   - A compiler path containing `#` is truncated in `override LLVM := ...`. Verified.
   - esc() only handles `$`.

3. **`$` in caller values.** The `:=` expansion of `$(MAKEOVERRIDES)` de-escapes `$$` once, so a caller's value containing `$` reaches the sub-make changed. Verified: `FOO=a$$b#c` came out as `a#c`.

4. **bzImage.unsigned.** Re-signing an image that carries another key's signature makes pesign append a second signature. `bzImage.unsigned` then holds a signed image. Verified.

5. **Old kernels.** Kernels 5.4 and older name the default target `_all`. `elkt-all: __all` would break a goal-less make there. From memory, not checked.

6. **Root and the hook.** A goal-less make run as root would create root's own key and add a second signature.

7. **Minor pin_text / pin_toolchain points.**
   - The pin_text docstring says ELKT_NO_PIN "switches it all off", but the sign hook stays on.
   - On a read-only tree pin_toolchain raises an uncaught PermissionError (a traceback).
   - A dangling symlink named GNUmakefile is overwritten.

Not verifiable here: on OpenSSL 1.1.1 (RHEL 8), `-addext basicConstraints` on top of the config's v3_ca section may produce a duplicate extension. OpenSSL 3.5 on this machine produces a clean certificate: CA:FALSE, digitalSignature, codeSigning.

Checked and sound:
- **Caller variables.** On a real 7.2.6 top Makefile copy and in miniatures, the pin wins against LLVM=1, LLVM=-21, CC=/HOSTCC=/LD=, `make -e`, CC/LD/LLVM in the environment, and variables arriving through a parent make's MAKEFLAGS. M= builds are pinned in the module directory.
- **Hook timing.** It runs exactly once, after `__all`, under -j. It stays off for goals, M=, ELKT_NO_SIGN and -n.
- **Shipping.** kernel-devel (install-extmod-build) ships only `Makefile`, so the GNUmakefile never reaches another machine. Both halves are guarded by $(wildcard) anyway.
- **Pin lifecycle.** The hook-only wrapper is kept when the system compiler is chosen with Secure Boot on. Authorship detection and the atomic rewrite are correct.
- **Key permissions.**
  - The key is created 0600 under umask 077, in a 0700 directory.
  - The PKCS#12 and the NSS database live in a 0700 mkdtemp and are removed in a finally block. Only a SIGKILL leaves them behind.
- **Signing tools.** The sbsign argv matches its CLI. pesign output mode is 0644. 3650-day validity is fine for shim.

findings.title: Signer is identified by CN substring only, and the package-time sign hook can use a different key directory than `package` does: a mismatched secureboot.der is published as verified
findings.location: scrubbed_env/ENV_KEEP (155-165), keys_dir (2565), signing_key CN (2585-2589), sign_image (2643-2645, 2666), install_preflight (2742), packaged_image_signed (3920), cmd_package (3945-3986)
findings.scenario:
Precondition: XDG_CONFIG_HOME points somewhere other than ~/.config. It is unset on this machine today, so this does not affect the current user yet.
1. `package` calls signing_key() in its own environment, which gives key A under $XDG_CONFIG_HOME.
2. It runs `make binrpm-pkg` with scrubbed_env(), which keeps HOME but drops XDG_CONFIG_HOME.
3. rpm's %build runs a goal-less make, so the GNUmakefile hook runs `tool.py sign --source TREE`.
4. In the hook, keys_dir() falls back to ~/.config, and signing_key(create=True) silently makes key B there. The "made a key" line goes into the package log only. The relinked image is signed with B.
5. A and B both have CN `user@host kernel signing key`, because USER and nodename are the same in both environments.
6. packaged_image_signed() does `cn in image_signers(...)`, which is True. The tool prints "the kernel image INSIDE ... is signed with '...'", copies key A's secureboot.der and writes INSTALL.txt telling the downloader to enrol it.
7. The published certificate does not verify the published image. With Secure Boot on, shim refuses it.

The same CN-only check causes two related problems:
- After the key files are regenerated (see PIN-3), `sign` says "was already signed" and install_preflight accepts an image signed by the old key.
- If key_cn() returns "" because the .crt is unparsable, `"" in output` is True. install_preflight and packaged_image_signed then accept an unsigned image.
findings.evidence:
I ran the real CLI in a scrubbed environment with a temp HOME, against a copy of /boot/vmlinuz-7.2.4-gpu, while the "parent" had XDG_CONFIG_HOME=S/xdgA.

Output:
  package's key (A): sha256 Fingerprint=A1:71:97:5F...
  hook's key    (B): sha256 Fingerprint=F6:55:C1:A1...
  pesign -S: ["The signer's common name is madness@siege3 kernel signing key"]
  key_cn(A) in image_signers(img): True
  sign_image(tree, A) -> already
  certificate actually embedded in the image: sha256 Fingerprint=F6:55:C1:A1...
  '' in image_signers(unsigned) -> True

Code:
  ENV_KEEP = ("HOME", "USER", "LOGNAME", "TERM", "TMPDIR", "SHELL", "CCACHE_DIR")
  line 2644: `if cn and cn in image_signers(img): return "already"`
  line 3920: `return cn in image_signers(os.path.join(dirpath, fn))`
findings.suggested_fix:
1. Add XDG_CONFIG_HOME and XDG_STATE_HOME to ENV_KEEP. Alternatively, have cmd_package pass the key directory to the hook in an env var that keys_dir() honours. The hook's sign should also call signing_key(create=False).
2. Compare the certificate, not the name. `pesign -i IMG -e sig.p7` followed by `openssl pkcs7 -inform DER -print_certs | openssl x509 -fingerprint -sha256`, compared with secureboot.crt's fingerprint, works with the tools already required. `sbverify --cert` does the same on the sbsign path. At minimum, give each new key a unique CN (random suffix) and treat an empty CN as "not signed".

findings.title: The pin splits MAKEOVERRIDES on blanks: with --ccache on the tool's own build does nothing and exits 0 (or fails at the first make), and other callers' values are mangled
findings.location: pin_text line 2507 (filter-out on $(MAKEOVERRIDES)); triggered by resolve_toolchain 1709-1713 (`CC=<ccache> <cc>`), Make.argv 1569-1571, cmd_build 3720/3764
findings.scenario:
GNU make stores a command-line value containing a blank as `CC=/usr/bin/ccache\ /usr/bin/gcc`, which is two words to $(filter-out).

1. With `--ccache on` the pin always has a CC entry. The tool then runs `make -j24 "CC=/usr/bin/ccache /usr/bin/gcc"` in the tree, so the make goes through the GNUmakefile it has just written.
2. The filter removes the word `CC=/usr/bin/ccache\` and leaves `/usr/bin/gcc` behind.
3. make 4.4.1 treats that stray word in MAKEFLAGS as a goal of the sub-make.

On a fresh tree: `make -s kernelversion` fails with "Configuration file .config not found", so `build` dies at once with a misleading error.

On a previously built tree: config targets still work, but the goal-less build prints "Nothing to be done for '/usr/bin/gcc'" and exits 0. The tool then reports "built in 0m00s", finds the old image "already signed", and with --install installs the stale kernel next to the new .config.

Even with the splitting fixed, the pin replaces CC with the bare compiler. The tool's own build would then run without ccache while reporting "ccache: on".

Other effects of the same line:
- Any caller variable whose value contains a word starting with CC=, LD=, LLVM= and so on is silently edited.
- When the removed word came last, the pinned assignment is glued into the previous variable's value.
findings.evidence:
Pin generated by pin_text() with ccache=True, dropped into a scratch copy of the real 7.2.6 top Makefile with a faked .config and auto.conf:
  $ make -j4 "CC=/usr/bin/ccache /usr/bin/gcc"
  make[1]: Nothing to be done for '/usr/bin/gcc'.
  exit=0

Same pin, fresh copy:
  $ make "CC=..." -s kernelversion
  *** Configuration file ".config" not found!
  exit=2
  (with ELKT_NO_PIN=1 the same command prints 7.2.6)

Minimal reproduction:
  top MAKEFLAGS=[ -- /usr/bin/gcc CC=/usr/bin/gcc]
  make[1]: Nothing to be done for '/usr/bin/gcc'.

Unrelated variable on the real top Makefile:
  $ make run-command KBUILD_RUN_COMMAND='@echo hello CC=1 world'
  hello world

ccache is not installed on this machine, which is why the user has not hit it.
findings.suggested_fix:
1. Hide escaped blanks before filtering and restore them afterwards:
   `elkt-sp := @@elkt-sp@@`
   `MAKEOVERRIDES := $(subst $(elkt-sp),\ ,$(filter-out ...,$(subst \ ,$(elkt-sp),$(MAKEOVERRIDES))))`
   Tested in the miniature: the build runs, and FOO=[hello CC=1 world] survives.
2. Set ELKT_NO_PIN=1 in scrubbed_env(). The tool passes its full toolchain on the command line anyway, so its own ccache CC is not replaced by the bare compiler.

findings.title: signing_key() overwrites the existing private key when only the .crt or .der is missing
findings.location: signing_key, lines 2579-2595
findings.scenario:
The key is persistent on purpose, because machines enrol its certificate in MOK once. The reuse test is `all(os.path.isfile(v) for v in k.values())` over .key, .crt and .der.

If the .der or .crt is missing, the code falls through to `openssl req -new -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 ... -keyout secureboot.key`. That writes a brand-new private key over the old one. There is no backup and no question; the only trace is the routine "made a Secure Boot signing key" line, which goes into the package log when the hook triggers it.

Plausible ways to get there:
- The user moves secureboot.der to a USB stick to enrol it elsewhere.
- The user restores only the .key from backup. The tool's own advice is "keep the .key private; back it up".

Outcome:
- Every machine that enrolled the old certificate rejects all future kernels.
- The old key is unrecoverable.
- Because the new CN is identical, existing images are reported as "already signed" by the new key (see PIN-1).

Related: signing_key(create=False) returns None in the same state, so install_preflight reports a correctly signed image as unsigned.
findings.evidence:
Experiment in a temp XDG_CONFIG_HOME:
  key A pub tail: 4eaedd08f35d6b0203010001
  (delete secureboot.der)
  create=False with .der missing -> None
  made a Secure Boot signing key: .../secureboot.key
  key after .der was deleted: ed06c37f17fde70203010001 -> private key REPLACED BY A NEW ONE

Code:
  `if all(os.path.isfile(v) for v in k.values()): return k`
  followed by an unconditional `openssl req ... -newkey rsa:2048 ... -keyout k["key"]`
findings.suggested_fix:
Never run `-newkey` when k["key"] exists.
- If the .key and .crt exist, regenerate only the .der with `openssl x509 -outform DER`.
- If only the .key exists, either rebuild the certificate from it (`openssl req -new -x509 -key <existing>`) or stop with a ToolError naming the missing file.

findings.title: The sign hook can never fire for bindeb-pkg (its build step has goals) or tarxz-pkg (it uses -f Makefile); `package --format deb` with Secure Boot on always fails and leaves the unsigned .deb in the publish directory
findings.location: pin_text hook lines 2522-2538 (the comment at 2523 and the condition at 2532); cmd_package 3947-3985
findings.scenario:
The hook is only active when MAKECMDGOALS is empty. The comment says "`make binrpm-pkg` / `bindeb-pkg` run a plain, goal-less `make`". That is true for the rpm spec only.

deb:
- scripts/package/debian/rules builds with `$(MAKE) $(make-opts) olddefconfig` and then `$(MAKE) $(make-opts) headers all`. Both have goals, so the hook stays off.
- mkdebian runs on every bindeb-pkg (`debian: FORCE`). It takes a fresh `scripts/build-version` number and passes it as KBUILD_BUILD_VERSION, so vmlinux is relinked and bzImage rewritten unsigned.
- On Debian/Ubuntu, where deb is the auto-selected format, `package` with the default --secure-boot on therefore always ends after the full run with "the kernel image inside ... is NOT signed -- not publishing it (... was it removed?)". The message blames a removed GNUmakefile.
- The packages were already copied into ~/kernel-packages/<release>/ at lines 3971-3972, before the check. An unsigned .deb is left there, possibly next to an earlier run's INSTALL.txt, secureboot.der and SHA256SUMS.

tar:
- tar-install runs `$(MAKE) -f $(srctree)/Makefile`, which bypasses the GNUmakefile.
- It does not relink, so it works only if the tree was already signed.
- A tree built with --secure-boot off, or by hand, fails late with the same misleading message, because cmd_package never signs itself.

findings.title: Key generation fails when user@hostname is longer than 45 characters (X.509 CN limit of 64), and only after the whole build
findings.location: signing_key lines 2585-2593; called from secure_boot_sign (2684) after run_build in cmd_build (3782)
findings.scenario:
CN = "<USER>@<nodename> kernel signing key", and the suffix alone is 19 characters.

On a host whose nodename is an FQDN the CN exceeds 64 characters. For example, AWS default names such as ec2-user@ip-172-31-23-45.eu-central-1.compute.internal give 72 characters. OpenSSL then refuses the -subj.

- In `build`, the key is first needed after the complete compile. The run ends in ERROR at the signing stage; post-build checks and --install never happen.
- The failed openssl call leaves an orphan secureboot.key behind.
- Every later attempt fails the same way.
- There is no option to choose the CN. The only ways out are --secure-boot off or faking USER.
findings.evidence:
Experiment with os.uname patched to that nodename and USER=ec2-user:
  long CN: ToolError: command failed (exit 1): openssl req -new -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 ... -subj /CN=ec2-user@ip-172-31-23-45.eu-central-1.compute.int...
  error:06800097:asn1 encoding routines:ASN1_mbstring_ncopy:string too long:crypto/asn1/a_mbstr.c:106:maxsize=64
  left behind: ['secureboot.key']
findings.suggested_fix:
- Truncate the identity so the CN fits, for example `who = who[:64 - len(" kernel signing key")]`.
- Create the key in the preflight (doctor, or before configure) when secure_boot is on, so that a key problem costs seconds rather than a build.

findings.title: On any non-x86_64 machine the default build ends in ERROR after compiling, and the installed hook makes every goal-less make in the tree fail
findings.location: image_path 2611-2614, sign_image 2638-2640, cmd_build 3720 and 3782-3785, doctor 3477
findings.scenario:
secure_boot defaults to "on" and nothing checks the architecture up front.

On aarch64, ppc64le, s390x, riscv64 or i686:
1. doctor passes if pesign is present. If it is absent, doctor demands a signing tool that would never be used.
2. cmd_build writes the sign hook into the tree at line 3720.
3. The full build runs.
4. secure_boot_sign() raises "image signing is implemented for x86_64 only, so far".
5. The exception lands in stage "checks". post_build_checks never runs, `build --install` never installs, and the command exits 1 after the whole compile.

The hook stays in the tree. A later goal-less `make` by hand, or rpm's %build during `package`, builds fine and then dies at the end with `[GNUmakefile: elkt-all] Error 1`.

arm64's Image is only a PE file with EFI_ZBOOT. That case is not handled at all, which is acceptable; failing late and breaking make is the bug.
findings.evidence:
Code:
  `rel = {"x86_64": "arch/x86/boot/bzImage"}.get(arch)` followed by `return ... if rel else ""`
  sign_image: `if not img: raise ToolError("image signing is implemented for x86_64 only, so far")`
  cmd_build: `if opts["secure_boot"] == "on": k = secure_boot_sign(tree, machine)` runs straight after the build, inside the try whose handler only records last_error and re-raises.
  pin_toolchain(tree, toolchain, opts["secure_boot"] == "on") writes the hook regardless of architecture.
findings.suggested_fix:
Decide once, before the build. If image_path(tree) is empty, warn "image signing is not available on <arch>; the config is Secure-Boot-ready but the image will be unsigned". In that case:
- skip secure_boot_sign
- call pin_toolchain with sign=False
- do not demand a signing tool in doctor

findings.title: Variables the pin leaves "loose" are only neutralised in kbuild's sub-make; when kbuild does not re-invoke itself, a caller's CC=, LD= or an exported LLVM= still win
findings.location: pin_text lines 2507-2517 (the MAKEOVERRIDES filter plus `unexport`); the claim is repeated in dkms_check 2349
findings.scenario:
For pinned variables `override` works in the first make. For every other name in PINNED_VARS the design relies on the MAKEOVERRIDES filter and `unexport`, which only affect a child make.

kbuild skips the sub-make in two cases:
- `--no-print-directory` is already in MAKEFLAGS. This was verified on the real 7.2.6 top Makefile.
- The top Makefile only recurses for O= builds. That describes 5.x LTS trees as I recall them (not checked here), and resolve_kernel accepts anything from 3.0 up.

In those cases, take a tree pinned to LLVM=/opt/clang24/bin/ that is built with `make -C tree M=... "CC=cc" "LD=ld"`. This is how NVIDIA's installer calls kbuild. The result is CC=cc and LD=ld with the clang-24 config, which is exactly the mismatch the pin exists to prevent.

The reverse also happens. A gcc-toolset pin (CC and HOSTCC pinned, LLVM loose) plus a shell that exports LLVM= gives CC=gcc with LD=ld.lld and the llvm-* tools. This machine's .bashrc exports LLVM=.

On 6.13 and later, M= builds always recurse, so DKMS against this user's 7.x trees is fine.
findings.evidence:
Real 7.2.6 top Makefile copy, pin = LLVM=S/fakecc/:
  $ make CC=cc LD=ld run-command KBUILD_RUN_COMMAND='@echo compiler:$(CC) linker:$(LD)'
  compiler:S/fakecc/clang linker:S/fakecc/ld.lld
  $ make --no-print-directory CC=cc LD=ld run-command ...
  compiler:cc linker:ld

Old-style miniature (no sub-make for an in-tree build):
  make -C tree_old M=... modules CC=cc LD=ld
    -> CC=cc LD=ld HOSTCC=S/fakecc/clang LLVM=S/fakecc/
  with a CC/HOSTCC pin and LLVM=/opt/x/ in the environment
    -> CC=S/fakecc/clang LD=/opt/x/ld.lld
findings.suggested_fix:
After the `unexport` line, also remove the loose names from this make:
  `$(foreach v,<loose names>,$(eval override undefine $(v)))`

Tested: the old-style miniature, the new-style miniature and the --no-print-directory case all then report the pinned clang and ld.lld. kbuild's own later `CC = ...` assignments still apply.

findings.title: dkms_check says "this tree pins its toolchain ... builds through it use <X>" for files that pin nothing, and names the compiler from the current command line rather than the pinned one
findings.location: dkms_check lines 2348-2350 (reached from cmd_dkms_check 4056, cmd_install 3842, cmd_pin 4048, post_build_checks)
findings.scenario:
The test is only `read_text(GNUmakefile).startswith(PIN_MARK)`.

findings.title: INSTALL.txt for the tar format tells the downloader to run `sudo tar -C / -xf`, which replaces the /lib symlink with a real directory on every usr-merged distro
findings.location: cmd_package, line 3992 (the "tar" entry of `steps`) in /home/madness/Documents/universal_linux_kernel_script/enterprise_linux_kernel_tool/enterprise_linux_kernel_tool.py
findings.scenario:
1. `package --format tar` (also the automatic choice where neither rpmbuild nor dpkg-deb exists, e.g. Arch). kbuild's cmd_tar runs `cd tar-install; tar cf ../linux-<rel>-x86_64.tar.xz --owner=root --group=root --sort=name *`, so the archive has the DIRECTORY members `boot/` and `lib/`.
2. INSTALL.txt tells the downloader: `sudo tar -C / -xf linux-<rel>-x86_64.tar.xz`.
3. On Fedora/EL, Debian, Ubuntu, Arch, openSUSE TW `/lib` is a symlink to `usr/lib`. GNU tar's default, when a directory member meets a symlink of the same name, is to REMOVE the symlink and create a directory.
4. Result: `/lib` becomes a real directory holding only `modules/<new release>`. `/lib/modules/<every other kernel>`, `/lib/firmware`, `/lib/udev`, `/lib/systemd` vanish from that path. On Debian/Ubuntu `/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2` points through `/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/`, so every dynamically linked program (sudo included) stops executing at once; on EL/Arch no kernel, old or new, can load a module after switch-root (vfat for /boot/efi -> emergency shell). The fallback kernel is broken too.
findings.evidence:
Line 3992: `"tar": "  sudo tar -C / -xf %s\n  sudo depmod %s && sudo dracut --kver %s ...`
Experiment in scratch (tarexp/), archive made with kbuild's exact tar command, fake root with `lib -> usr/lib`, GNU tar 1.35:
  before: `lrwxrwxrwx lib -> usr/lib`
  `tar -C fakeroot -xf linux-9.9.9-elkt-x86_64.tar.xz`  exit=0
  after:  `drwxr-xr-x lib`  (contains only modules/); usr/lib/modules still holds only OLD
Same archive with `--keep-directory-symlink`: `lib -> usr/lib` survives and usr/lib/modules holds `9.9.9-elkt OLD`.
This machine: `/lib -> usr/lib`, `/lib64 -> usr/lib64`.
findings.suggested_fix: Line 3992: `sudo tar -C / --keep-directory-symlink --no-overwrite-dir -xf %s` (GNU tar >= 1.27; --no-overwrite-dir also stops it re-moding /boot). Say in the same line that it needs GNU tar.

findings.title: The 'is it signed' check matches the certificate's CN only, and the sign hook looks for the key in a different place than `package` does: an image signed by ANOTHER key is published next to your secureboot.der and reported as verified
findings.location: packaged_image_signed line 3920 (`return cn in image_signers(...)`); cmd_package lines 3945, 3978, 3986; scrubbed_env/ENV_KEEP lines 155-165; keys_dir line 2565; signing_key line 2579-2583; sign_image line 2644
findings.scenario:

1. `package` runs in the user's environment: keys_dir() = $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/enterprise_linux_kernel_tool/keys -> key A; its .der is what line 3986 publishes.
2. make gets scrubbed_env(): ENV_KEEP has HOME but no XDG_*. rpmbuild's %build runs the GNUmakefile hook `python3 -I tool sign --source $(CURDIR)`; there keys_dir() = ~/.config/... ; no key there, so signing_key(create=True) silently MINTS key B (same CN, because CN = user@host) and signs the relinked bzImage with it.
3. Line 3978 checks `key_cn(A) in pesign -S output` -> True. Output: "ok the kernel image INSIDE ... is signed with '<CN>'", secureboot.der (A) published.
4. Downloader enrols A, enables Secure Boot; shim refuses the kernel.
Trigger B (no XDG needed): keys directory recreated (any of the 3 files missing -> signing_key regenerates all, same CN). A tree signed earlier with the old key: sign_image returns 'already' (line 2644, CN match), the tar path never relinks, the check passes, the NEW .der ships with an OLD-key image.
Also: key_cn() returns '' when openssl cannot parse the .crt, and `'' in text` is True: an unsigned image passes.
findings.evidence:
Reproduced end to end in scratch (xdgexp/, temp HOME, temp XDG_CONFIG_HOME, copy of elkt-test's bzImage.unsigned):
  package side: `keys_dir seen by package: .../xdg/enterprise_linux_kernel_tool/keys`, `env handed to make has XDG_CONFIG_HOME: False`
  hook run exactly as the recipe does, in scrubbed_env: `made a Secure Boot signing key: .../home/.config/enterprise_linux_kernel_tool/keys/secureboot.key` then `ok arch/x86/boot/bzImage is signed with 'madness@siege3 kernel signing key'`
  `packaged_image_signed('tar', pkg, key_cn(A)) -> True`
  cert embedded in the image (pesign -e | openssl pkcs7 -print_certs): sha256 63:96:53:55:...  vs. the secureboot.der that would be published: F9:97:0B:DC:...
  `packaged_image_signed('tar', <unsigned image>, '') -> True`
findings.suggested_fix: (1) Compare the certificate, not the name: export the embedded cert (`pesign -i IMG -e sig.p7` + `openssl pkcs7 -inform DER -print_certs | openssl x509 -noout -fingerprint -sha256`, or `sbverify --cert k['crt'] IMG`) and require it to equal k['der']'s fingerprint; treat an empty CN as 'not signed'. Use that helper in packaged_image_signed, sign_image's 'already' test and install_preflight. (2) Add XDG_CONFIG_HOME (and XDG_STATE_HOME) to ENV_KEEP, or write the absolute keys directory into the GNUmakefile recipe; and make the hook path use signing_key(create=False) so an unattended build step can never mint a key.

findings.title: The re-sign hook only fires for a goal-less make without -f: bindeb-pkg (`make ... headers all`) and tarxz-pkg (`make -f Makefile`) never re-sign, so `--format deb` can never succeed with Secure Boot on, and tar fails after any rpm run

Every `package --format deb` with the default --secure-boot on ends in 'the kernel image inside ... is NOT signed ... (The tree's GNUmakefile signs after the package's build step; was it removed?)' -- a wrong diagnosis; nothing the user can do fixes it.

  deb         `make ... KBUILD_BUILD_VERSION=6 headers all` -> headers, relink -- NO sign line

findings.title: No per-tree lock: a second build on a tree that is being built right now treats the live 'building' record as a kill -9 and runs mrproper under the running make
findings.location: cmd_build lines 3697-3718 (decide_clean call, state.update 'configuring', clean_tree); decide_clean lines 2108-2110; State.update lines 2052-2053 (the only flock in the file)
findings.scenario:
A build is running in tree T, so state.ini says status=building. This is the state of ~/src/linux-7.2.6 right now. Someone starts `build --profile X` or the wizard on T from another terminal. The wizard path is Enter (newest profile), Enter (use as is), Enter (Proceed).
1. prev.status is 'building', so decide_clean('auto', True, 'building', ...) returns clean=True with the reason 'the last run recorded building and never recorded an end (kill -9, OOM or power loss)'.
2. state.update then overwrites the live run's record with 'configuring'.
3. clean_tree runs `make mrproper` in the tree while the first instance's -j24 make is compiling in it.
4. The second instance then configures and builds in the same tree alongside the first.

The tool has no way to tell a stale 'building' from a live one: it records no pid, and the flock is held only for the milliseconds of State.update. In the wizard the 'Proceed?' prompt (line 3685) comes before the 'Previous attempt / cleaning' lines (3692-3705), so the user confirms without seeing that a clean is planned. Non-interactive `build` asks nothing.

install, package, sign and pin with --source also never check for status=building, so they will run make or install from a tree that is mid-build. With the live profile (install=yes, set_default=yes), whichever of two racing instances ends with rc=0 installs its result and makes it the default boot entry.
findings.evidence:
Experiment in <scratch>/exp1: a miniature tree whose default target sleeps 25 s, with two real instances of the tool started 12 s apart. Instance 2 printed:
  recorded    : building at stage build
  cleaning    : the last run recorded 'building' and never recorded an end (kill -9, OOM or power loss)
  saved       : .config -> .config.before-clean
The tree's trace file:
  build-start 07:53:41
  MRPROPER-RAN 07:53:53
  build-start 07:53:53
  build-end 07:54:06
  build-end 07:54:18
Both instances then reported 'ok   built in 0m25s'.
`grep -n flock` on the tool finds only line 2053, inside State.update.
findings.suggested_fix:
At the top of cmd_build, before prev is used, take a non-blocking per-tree lock and hold it for the life of the process:
  lock = open(os.path.join(sdir, 'tree-' + hashlib.sha256(tree.encode()).hexdigest()[:16] + '.lock'), 'w')
  fcntl.flock(lock, fcntl.LOCK_EX | fcntl.LOCK_NB)
On failure raise ToolError('another instance is working on <tree>').

The kernel drops the flock on kill -9, so 'building' with the lock free still means a dead run. Python opens the file with O_CLOEXEC, so make does not inherit it. Take the same lock in cmd_install, cmd_package, cmd_sign and cmd_pin. Also print the clean decision before the wizard's 'Proceed?'.

verdict.reasoning:
I traced the path and found no guard that stops it, then reproduced it.

- **State read:** cmd_build line 3669 does `prev = state.get(tree)`.
- **Clean decision:** lines 3703-3704 call `decide_clean(opts["clean"], has_objects, prev.get("status", ""), ..., in_service(tree))`. decide_clean lines 2108-2110 read `elif status == "building": want, why = True, ("the last run recorded 'building' and never recorded an end ...")`.
- **Record overwritten:** line 3713 overwrites the live run's record with `status="configuring"`.
- **mrproper:** lines 3717-3718 call `clean_tree`, which runs `mk.call(["mrproper"])`.
- **Locking:** the only flock in the file is inside State.update (lines 2052-2053). It is held only for the duration of the write. No pid is recorded anywhere.
- **The one guard:** decide_clean lines 2120-2126 return `False, msg + " -- NOT cleaning"` when the tree is in service. For the live tree that applied only from 08:07, when the first install created /lib/modules/7.2.6-xeon-haswell-all-gpu-server-latency/build. During the 33-minute build it did not apply. Even with that guard, the second instance still configures and builds in the same tree alongside the first.
- **Wizard order:** confirmed by reading. `Proceed?` is at line 3685. The 'Previous attempt / cleaning' lines come after it, at 3692-3705.

On severity: the scenario needs a second start on the same tree, which is user error. But the wizard is the default command, and three Enters get there. The cost is a destroyed multi-hour build. With the live profile (install=yes, set_default=yes), whichever racing instance ends with rc=0 is installed as the default boot entry.

The finder's suggested fix has a side effect. Taking the same non-blocking lock in cmd_sign breaks `package` with Secure Boot on, which is the default. The pinned GNUmakefile's `elkt-all` recipe (pin_text lines 2530-2538) runs `<tool> sign --source $(CURDIR)` as a descendant of the make that cmd_package started. cmd_package passes ELKT_NO_SIGN="" (line 3955), so that nested sign does run, and it would be refused while cmd_package holds the lock.

All runs were in <scratch>/bld1, on a miniature tree whose default target sleeps 10 s, with env -i and HOME/XDG/--state-dir redirected. Two real instances were started 5 s apart.

While instance 1 built, state.ini showed `status = building`. Instance 2 printed:

  cleaning    : the last run recorded 'building' and never recorded an end (kill -9, OOM or power loss)

The tree's trace file:

  MRPROPER-RAN 08:12:43
  build-start 08:12:43
  build-end 08:12:48
  build-end 08:12:53

Fix validation on a scratch copy (<scratch>/patched):
- All 111 unit tests still pass.
- The second instance exits with 'ERROR: another enterprise_linux_kernel_tool is working in <tree> right now'.

- After kill -9 of the tool and its make, the next run still prints "cleaning: the last run recorded 'building'". So a dead run is still told apart from a live one.
verdict.minimal_fix:
Add a helper next to now():

  _TREE_LOCKS = []
  def lock_tree(tree):
      if os.environ.get("ELKT_TREE_LOCKED"): return      # a `sign` started by the tree's own GNUmakefile, under `package`
      try: f = open(os.path.join(tree, ".elkt-lock"), "a")
      except (OSError, IOError): return
      try: fcntl.flock(f, fcntl.LOCK_EX | fcntl.LOCK_NB)
      except (OSError, IOError):
          f.close(); raise ToolError("another %s is working in %s right now" % (TOOL, tree))
      _TREE_LOCKS.append(f)                               # held for the life of the process

- Call it in cmd_build just before `sdir = state_dir(opts)`, which is before `prev` is read.
- Call it in cmd_install, cmd_sign and cmd_package right after built_tree().
- In cmd_package, pass `"ELKT_TREE_LOCKED": "1"` in run_build's extra_env. Without this the GNUmakefile's re-sign step is refused and packaging fails.
- Keep the lock file in the tree, not the state dir. Two instances given different --state-dir then still exclude each other. mrproper's patterns do not match `.elkt-lock`.
- The code is Python 3.6 safe. open() is O_CLOEXEC, so make and sudo do not inherit the lock. The kernel drops it on kill -9, so 'building' with the lock free still means a dead run.
- Optionally move the 'Previous attempt / cleaning' block above the wizard's `Proceed?` prompt.

findings.title: In-service protection stops at mrproper: building another profile in a tree that /lib/modules/<rel>/build points at swaps the pin, .config and kernel.release under the installed kernel

All three profiles use kernel=7.2.6 and workdir=~/src, so they all build in ~/src/linux-7.2.6. The running build has install=yes and set_default=yes. When it finishes, /lib/modules/7.2.6-xeon-haswell-all-gpu-server-latency/build points at that tree, and that kernel is the default boot entry.

Next the user runs `build --profile machine-native-gpu` (gcc), which is what the earlier advice 'build the downloadable kernel with the system gcc' leads to.
1. decide_clean says 'finished cleanly (installed); incremental is correct', and the build proceeds.
2. Line 3720 rewrites GNUmakefile for the new toolchain, so the clang-24 pin is gone before configure has even run. It stays gone if the run then fails verification, is interrupted with ^C, or was --configure-only.

findings.title: main() replaces an ignored SIGHUP with its own handler, so `nohup tool build &` is aborted at logout, and make loses the ignore too
findings.location: main lines 4194-4195: `for sig in (signal.SIGTERM, signal.SIGHUP): signal.signal(sig, _as_interrupt)`
findings.scenario:
The user starts a one-to-two-hour build with `nohup ./enterprise_linux_kernel_tool.py build --profile X &` and logs out, or the ssh session drops.
1. nohup sets SIGHUP to SIG_IGN before exec. main() installs _as_interrupt over it unconditionally.
2. The shell forwards SIGHUP at hangup. The handler raises KeyboardInterrupt, and run_build's handler terminates make.
3. State becomes failed/build with exit 130. The build the user explicitly protected is lost.

A caught signal is reset to default at exec, while an ignored one stays ignored. So the make child has also lost nohup's protection.
findings.evidence:
Experiment in <scratch>/exp1: `( trap '' HUP; exec ./run.sh ... ) &`, which is what nohup does. While the build was running:
  tool /proc/PID/status:  SigIgn: 0000000001001000   SigCgt: 0000000000004003   (bit 0, SIGHUP, is no longer ignored and is now caught)
  make child:             SigIgn: 0000000000000000
After `kill -HUP <tool pid>`:
  tool exit code: 130
  interrupted -- the tree is consistent; re-running continues incrementally.
  status = failed / stage = build / exit_code = 130
The trace shows build-start and no build-end.

verdict.reasoning:
main() lines 4194-4195 are unconditional: `for sig in (signal.SIGTERM, signal.SIGHUP): signal.signal(sig, _as_interrupt)`. Nothing checks the inherited disposition.

- Python leaves an inherited SIG_IGN for SIGHUP alone. The control run shows getsignal(SIGHUP) == SIG_IGN at start under `trap '' HUP`.
- The tool then replaces the ignore that nohup set up with a handler that raises KeyboardInterrupt.
- When a terminal or ssh session drops, bash gets SIGHUP and re-sends it to every job, nohup'd or not.
- The tool then runs run_build's `except BaseException` path, terminates make, and cmd_build lines 3804-3805 write status=failed / exit_code=130.
- A caught signal is reset to default at exec, while an ignored one stays ignored. So the make child loses nohup's protection too, and SIGHUP kills it directly.

The comment above the loop shows the handler was meant for the run without nohup ("A dropped ssh session is a SIGHUP ... state stays 'building'"). That purpose is kept by skipping only an inherited ignore.

findings.title: A SIGTERM to the tool alone (or any internal error in run_build) stops only the top-level make: recipe shells die and their compilers finish as orphans, leaving an object that skipped post-processing, which the next incremental run accepts
findings.location: run_build lines 2195-2198 (Popen without its own process group) and 2238-2252 (proc.terminate() signals only make); main line 4213 ('the tree is consistent')
findings.scenario:
The user runs `kill <tool pid>`, or a supervisor signals only the main pid, or the log write fails with ENOSPC. Any of these enters the `except BaseException` path.
1. proc.terminate() sends SIGTERM to the top make. make forwards it to its children, which are sub-makes and the /bin/sh -c of each recipe. make deletes partial targets.
2. kbuild recipes are compound: 'set -e; echo; $(CC) ...; objtool ...; fixdep ...'. The shell dies and the compiler it was waiting for is orphaned. The compiler finishes and writes foo.o after make's cleanup. objtool and fixdep never run for that object.
3. The tool reports 'interrupted -- the tree is consistent', and state becomes failed/build. The next run says 'make could tidy up; retrying incrementally'.

If an older .foo.o.cmd with the same command line exists, which is any rebuild of an existing object, kbuild treats foo.o as up to date. It is linked without ORC, retpoline or static-call site data for that file. A terminal ^C does not have this problem, because the tty signals the whole group.
findings.evidence:
Experiment in <scratch>/exp6: the recipe was `set -e; echo CC; ( sleep 10; echo ... > $@ ); echo OBJTOOL; echo post-processed >> $@`, and SIGTERM was sent to the python pid only.
  tool exit code: 130, 'interrupted -- the tree is consistent'
  `pgrep` still showed 'sleep 10' running
  afterwards init/main.o contained only 'object written by an ORPHANED compiler at 07:59:04', with no 'post-processed' line
The re-run printed:
  keeping : the last run failed at stage 'build' where make could tidy up; retrying incrementally
  ok   built in 0m00s: 0 steps
The object was unchanged. The miniature has no .cmd check. It stands in for kbuild's case where an old .cmd with an identical command exists.
findings.suggested_fix:
Start make in its own session and signal the whole group on the abort path:
  Popen(..., start_new_session=True)
and in the except handler use
  os.killpg(proc.pid, signal.SIGTERM)
instead of proc.terminate(), with os.killpg(proc.pid, signal.SIGKILL) after the timeout. ^C then also travels through that handler, because make is no longer in the terminal's foreground group.

verdict.reasoning:
The harm mechanism depends on kbuild recipes being a bare `set -e; echo; $(CC) ...; objtool ...; fixdep ...`, whose shell dies on SIGTERM and orphans the compiler. That is not what kbuild runs.

The guard is in the kernel tree, not the tool. /home/madness/src/linux-7.2.6/scripts/Kbuild.include lines 147-153:

  delete-on-interrupt = \
      $(if $(filter-out $(PHONY), $@), \
          $(foreach sig, HUP INT QUIT TERM PIPE, \
              trap 'rm -f $@; trap - $(sig); kill -s $(sig) $$$$' $(sig);))
  cmd = @$(if $(cmd_$(1)),set -e; $($(quiet)log_print) $(delete-on-interrupt) $(cmd_$(1)),:)

- cmd_cc_o_c, including `$(cmd_objtool)` (scripts/Makefile.lib lines 266-268), runs through `cmd` via cmd_and_fixdep (Kbuild.include lines 206-209). So every object recipe carries the trap.
- POSIX shells run a trap only after the foreground command has completed. On SIGTERM the recipe shell therefore does not die. It waits for the compiler, then removes the target, then kills itself.
- GNU make sends SIGTERM to its children and waits for them. The tool's proc.communicate() reads to EOF, so the tool also waits until the pipe's last writer is gone, or 60 s.
- Sub-makes are direct children (`$(Q)$(MAKE) $(build)=$@` is a simple command that make execs without a shell), so they are signalled recursively.

The finder's miniature left the trap out. Its own note says 'The miniature has no .cmd check'. With the trap added verbatim, the orphan object disappears.

What remains true:
- proc.terminate() signals only the top make.
- The line 'the tree is consistent' is kept true by kbuild's trap, not by the tool.
- A kernel old enough to predate delete-on-interrupt would behave as the finder describes. Every kernel I could check here has it; I could not check offline when it was introduced.

The finder's suggested fix (start_new_session plus killpg) is not needed for correctness. It would also change ^C and ^Z handling for every build.
verdict.experiment:
Make-level test in <scratch>/bld7-make (GNU make 4.4.1; /bin/sh is bash). A fake compiler sleeps 4 s and then writes $@. The recipe is `set -e; echo CC; <trap>; ./fakecc $@; echo OBJTOOL; echo post-processed >> $@`. SIGTERM was sent to make only.

- Without the trap (the finder's miniature): make exited at once, and 4 s later a.o held 'written by the compiler' with no 'post-processed' line. This reproduces the finder's observation.

Tool-level test in <scratch>/bld7-notrap and <scratch>/bld7-kbuildtrap: a real `build` on a miniature tree, with SIGTERM sent to the python pid only.
- Both exited 130 with 'interrupted -- the tree is consistent'.
- Both exited 3.5 s after the signal, when the fake compiler finished.
- notrap: 7 s later, init/main.o held 'object written by the compiler at 08:14:37' with no post-processing.
- kbuildtrap: 7 s later, 'cat: init/main.o: No such file or directory'.

findings.title: --keep-symbol is not saved in a profile, and 'CONFIG_' is stripped everywhere in the symbol name, so a replayed trimmed profile silently drops modules the user asked to keep
findings.location: merge_options lines 3077-3078; PROFILE_KEYS line 2912; save_profile lines 3026-3031; load_profile line 2955
findings.scenario:
1. The user runs `build --modules trimmed --keep-symbol NFS_FS --save-profile box`. The kernel has nfs as a module.
2. Later they run `build --profile box`, or use the wizard and 'use it as it is'. The documentation says this 'replays one without a single question'.
3. keep_symbols is not a DEFAULTS key, so it was never written to the profile and comes back as []. localmodconfig trims NFS_FS away unless nfs happens to be loaded at that moment. module_coverage only checks modules that are loaded now, so nothing warns. The missing module shows up after the reboot.

Separately, `s.upper().replace("CONFIG_", "")` removes every occurrence of 'CONFIG_', not just a leading one. `--keep-symbol CONFIG_IKCONFIG_PROC` becomes 'IKPROC', which is not a Kconfig symbol. It is skipped as 'not in this kernel version'.
findings.evidence:
<scratch>/exp7/t.py:
  run 1 keep_symbols : ['NFS_FS', 'IKPROC']      (given: NFS_FS and CONFIG_IKCONFIG_PROC)
  the saved profile has no keep_symbol line
  replay keep_symbols: []  modules: trimmed
findings.suggested_fix: Persist the list. Write 'keep_symbols = A,B' in save_profile, accept the key in load_profile, and in merge_options merge the profile's list with the command line's. Strip only a leading prefix: `s = s.upper(); s = s[7:] if s.startswith('CONFIG_') else s`.

verdict.reasoning:
- merge_options lines 3077-3078 build keep_symbols only from the command line: `getattr(args, "keep_symbol", None)`.
- PROFILE_KEYS is sorted(DEFAULTS) (line 2912), and 'keep_symbols' is not a DEFAULTS key.
- save_profile (3026-3031) writes only PROFILE_KEYS and PROFILE_FLAGS.
- load_profile (2955) filters to `k in DEFAULTS or k in PROFILE_FLAGS`.

So the list is never written to a profile and never read back. A replayed trimmed profile gets `[]`. build_requests line 1374 then adds only RESCUE_SYMBOLS. module_coverage checks only modules loaded at build time, so nothing warns about the dropped symbol.

Separately, `s.upper().replace("CONFIG_", "")` removes every occurrence, not just a leading one. This is worse than the finder said, because a symbol typed without the prefix is mangled too:
- IKCONFIG_PROC becomes IKPROC.
- BOOT_CONFIG_EMBED becomes BOOT_EMBED.

The mangled name is not in kconfig_symbols, so configure() skips it (`if r.sym in symbols`). report_verify then prints the misleading 'not in this kernel version'.

Low. --keep-symbol is a niche option. Few symbols contain 'CONFIG_', and those that do are rarely the modules one keeps through a trim.
verdict.experiment:
In <scratch>/bld8/t.py, with HOME and XDG redirected. The command was `build --modules trimmed --keep-symbol NFS_FS --keep-symbol CONFIG_IKCONFIG_PROC --keep-symbol BOOT_CONFIG_EMBED --save-profile box`.

  run 1 keep_symbols : ['NFS_FS', 'IKPROC', 'BOOT_EMBED']

- The saved box.ini has no keep-symbol line. grep finds only 'hz = keep' and 'preempt = keep', and `grep -c NFS` gives 0.
- Replay with `--profile box`:

  replay keep_symbols: []  modules: trimmed
  NFS_FS requested on replay: False

Fix validation on the patched copy: all 111 unit tests pass, including test_a_profile_holds_what_was_asked_not_what_it_resolved_to.
verdict.minimal_fix:
Keep the key out of DEFAULTS. It holds a list, and DEFAULTS values are strings that also drive PROFILE_KEYS, the command-line merge loop and validate_options.

- save_profile, after the PROFILE_FLAGS loop:
    if opts.get("keep_symbols"): cp.set("build", "keep_symbols", ",".join(opts["keep_symbols"]))
- load_profile: change the filter to `if k in DEFAULTS or k in PROFILE_FLAGS or k == "keep_symbols"`.
- merge_options, replacing lines 3077-3078:
    keep = (getattr(args, "keep_symbol", None) or []) + prof.get("keep_symbols", "").replace(",", " ").split()
    keep = [s.upper()[7:] if s.upper().startswith("CONFIG_") else s.upper() for s in keep]
    opts["keep_symbols"] = sorted(set(keep), key=keep.index)
